title: What Is Digital Rupee (e₹)? How It Works and How It Differs from Cryptocurrency
summary: Understand digital rupee meaning, how e₹ works, CBDC in India, and digital rupee vs cryptocurrency, with wallet steps, UPI differences and safety tips.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) began a trial program for its Central Bank Digital Currency, or CBDC, in December 2022. It is digital legal money, known as the digital rupee or e₹. Let’s go through the details and how you can use it.


### TL;DR


- The digital rupee, or e₹, is India’s central bank digital currency issued by the RBI. ₹1 in e₹ equals ₹1 in physical currency.
- Eligible users can load, pay, receive and redeem e₹ through participating providers’ wallets. Wallet balances do not earn interest.
- e₹ is sovereign money. Cryptocurrency is a different category of digital asset, while UPI is a payment system.


##


What Is a Digital Rupee? Digital Rupee Meaning and e₹ Meaning


The electronic rupee is a digital token that functions as legal currency. It is exchangeable one-for-one with physical rupees and can be accepted as a payment method and used as a store of value.


The digital rupee differs from cryptocurrencies because it is issued by the RBI at the same value as paper currency and coins. Digital currency is offered in amounts of ₹1, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20, ₹50 and other physical cash denominations.


**e₹ means electronic rupee** , commonly called the digital rupee. **CBDC means Central Bank Digital Currency** . Retail CBDC serves individuals and merchants; wholesale CBDC is tested for settlements between banks and other financial institutions.


##


How Does Digital Rupee Work?


The digital currency was issued by the RBI and distributed primarily by four banking institutions in the initial phase (pilot): the State Bank of India (SBI), IDFC First Bank, ICICI Bank and Yes Bank. RBI creates and issues e₹; participating intermediaries provide customer wallets and related services.


Customers can get a digital rupee from participating institutions and use it to execute transactions. To use the digital rupee, download digital wallets offered by participating providers onto your phone. Use only the official app. Unlike a cryptocurrency wallet, this wallet holds RBI-issued digital cash.


The digital rupee can be used to send money to another person or to pay bills where accepted. Payments to stores and merchants can also be made using[QR codes](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-qr-code/) , including supported UPI QR codes scanned through an e₹ app.


You will not receive interest on the digital rupee because it is similar to actual currency. Furthermore, much like actual cash, you still have the ability to convert it into other forms and transfer its value to a savings account, make a bank deposit, and so on, through supported redemption.


The digital rupee is the RBI’s digital form of sovereign currency. Its value and issuance come from the central bank, rather than cryptocurrency mining or trading.


### How to Start Using an e₹ Wallet


Follow your participating provider’s instructions. The usual process is:


1. **Check eligibility:** Confirm that the provider offers an e₹ wallet to you and that your device is supported.
2. **Download the official app:** Use the app-store link provided by the bank or authorised wallet provider.
3. **Register and verify:** Complete mobile verification and the onboarding steps shown. Requirements can differ by provider and use case.
4. **Load digital rupees:** Choose the load option and add the amount through a supported funding method.
5. **Pay or receive:** Use the wallet’s send, receive or scan-and-pay feature. Check the recipient and amount before confirming.
6. **Redeem when needed:** Use the redeem option to move the value back to your linked bank account, following the provider’s process.


For instance,[SBI’s digital rupee guidance](https://sbi.bank.in/web/personal-banking/digital/cbdc) explains registration, loading and redemption for its wallet. Do not assume every provider uses identical menu labels or limits.


##


What Is Cryptocurrency?


Simply put, Bitcoin is digital money that is not controlled by any government or central bank. It is designed and developed on blockchain technology and uses cryptography to protect transactions, making them difficult to falsify.


The goal of Bitcoin’s inception was to make it easier for users to transmit money over the internet. It is digital money and a payment mechanism, but it does not function precisely like traditional currencies in every legal or practical respect.


Some cryptocurrencies are generated through a time-consuming process called mining. Miners employ computers equipped with specialised hardware to solve challenging cryptographic problems in exchange for cryptocurrency rewards.


***Not all cryptocurrencies are mined:** Ethereum, for example, uses proof-of-stake validators instead.*


Cryptocurrency governance, issuance and backing vary. Bitcoin has no central issuer, while other digital tokens can have identifiable issuers. Their prices and risks also differ. However, is the digital rupee a cryptocurrency? Here’s some context for you.


##


Digital Rupee vs Cryptocurrency: Know the Difference


CBDC, as a digital form of national money, differs from privately issued cryptocurrencies in the following ways.


A CBDC is a legal currency produced by a central bank in digital form. This is the same as fiat cash and may be exchanged for it one-for-one. Just the structure is different. However, CBDCs should not be directly equated with cryptocurrencies.


CBDCs are not commodities or claims on commodities. Cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin do not have a central issuer; other cryptoassets can have issuers. These distinctions matter when comparing their backing and governance.


The CBDC is a digital representation of actual money issued by a central bank such as the RBI that can be easily converted into cash or bank deposits. The digital rupee is not a speculative cryptoasset since it is a currency issued by the RBI.


The currency’s governance and administration are in the hands of the central bank issuing the digital rupee. The digital rupee is a legal currency, which implies it can be used to purchase goods and services where accepted.


**Feature** **Digital rupee, or e₹** **Cryptocurrency**


Issuance Issued by the RBI. Depends on the asset; Bitcoin has no central issuer.


Status in India Legal tender and an RBI liability. Does not have the same sovereign-currency status as e₹.


Value in rupees ₹1 of e₹ equals ₹1. Market value depends on the asset; some tokens target a peg.


Creation Issued under the central bank’s currency framework. May use mining, staking or other issuance arrangements.


Holding and use Held in participating e₹ wallets for payments and transfers. Held or accessed through crypto wallets and platforms.


##


Digital Rupee vs UPI: Are They the Same?


The digital rupee is money, while[UPI is a payment system](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/upi-full-form-meaning-how-it-works/) . With a regular bank-account-funded UPI payment, money moves through the linked bank accounts. With an e₹ wallet, you hold digital rupees separately from your bank deposit.


For transfers between e₹ wallets, settlement happens without passing through the users’ bank accounts. Scanning a UPI QR code from an e₹ wallet uses interoperability, and the settlement follows the applicable UPI timelines. This does not turn every UPI app into an e₹ wallet.


Similarly,[digital wallets](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/types-of-e-wallets/) can hold different forms of value. An ordinary prepaid-wallet balance and an RBI-issued digital rupee are distinct. Bank transfers through[NEFT, RTGS or IMPS](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/imps-vs-neft-vs-rtgs/) also remain separate payment arrangements.


##


CBDC in India: List of Banks and Cities in the Digital Rupee Pilot


The RBI has expanded the digital currency pilot in a phased manner. The original launch plan and current availability are outlined below.


### Original Pilot Banks and Cities


The four banks engaged in the initial trial program were SBI, ICICI Bank, Yes Bank and IDFC First Bank. Expansions were planned in a phased manner. The second round of the trial program was to include four additional banks, which were: Bank of Baroda, Kotak Mahindra Bank, HDFC Bank and Union Bank of India.


The digital money was offered in four cities during the initial test phase: Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and Bhubaneswar. Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Hyderabad, Indore, Gangtok, Guwahati, Kochi, Patna and Shimla were listed for the second trial phase.


### Current Availability


The original pilot announcement did not give a timeframe for when the services would be offered in all locations and at all banks. Those bank and city lists describe launch history. The[RBI’s digital rupee FAQs](https://rbi.org.in/SCRIPTs/FAQDisplay.aspx?Id=169) , updated in October 2026, continue to describe retail and wholesale pilots and list participating banks and non-bank providers.


Check that list and your provider’s eligibility instructions before downloading an app. Availability of a wallet, onboarding requirements and features should be confirmed with the provider; access is not limited to the four original cities.


##


Is the Digital Rupee Safe to Use?


Customers shouldn’t compare the digital rupee to other virtual currencies (cryptocurrencies) merely because both use digital wallets. As far as its legitimacy is concerned, the Central Bank (RBI) issues it. Therefore, it has the same degree of confidence as actual cash in terms of sovereign backing.


Certainly, there may be some challenges with using digital money during the pilot. Nonetheless, the Reserve Bank of India has stated that the trial will be used to learn and that it will test different features and applications for customers based on the findings.


Follow basic[online payment security](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/online-payment-security/) practices: protect your phone and wallet credentials, avoid sharing OTPs and verify the recipient before confirming. If a payment remains unresolved, use the wallet provider’s support process and retain the transaction details.


##


Benefits and Limitations of Digital Rupee


Cash allocation and monitoring are challenging in India. CBDC may reduce some costs associated with operations, printing, distribution and storage of physical cash. It can add another payment option alongside existing[digital payment systems](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/digital-payment-system/) .


Cross-border fund transfers and currency conversions are time-consuming and costly. With the introduction of the digital rupee, faster cross-border money transfers are a potential avenue to improve bank cash management and operations. A domestic e₹ wallet does not automatically provide unrestricted international transfers.


The pilot also explores features such as offline payments and programmability. Availability depends on the provider and use case. Users should check wallet limits, accepted payment flows and support arrangements before relying on a feature.


##


Conclusion


The RBI thinks that by adopting the digital rupee, it could address issues with existing physical money and cross-border activities. These are potential benefits being tested, rather than guaranteed outcomes for every transaction.


For users, the digital rupee meaning is straightforward: it is RBI-issued money in a digital wallet. It can be used for supported payments, does not earn interest and can be redeemed through the provider’s process. Understanding how digital rupee works helps you choose when to use it alongside UPI and other payment methods.
